author: im-nick-adams
text:
m4t.remove handler crashes with "Channel has been closed" during extension host shutdown

## Bug Report

### Description

During extension host shutdown, when a tool registered via `vscode.lm.registerTool()` is disposed, Copilot Chat's internal `m4t.remove` handler attempts to log a debug message via a debug channel that has already been closed by the extension host. This produces an unhandled promise rejection on every shutdown.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Have an extension that registers language model tools via `vscode.lm.registerTool()`
2. Close the Extension Development Host window

### Error Output

```
rejected promise not handled within 1 second: Error: Channel has been closed
stack trace: Error: Channel has been closed
	at i (extensionHostProcess.js:501:3935)
	at Object.debug (extensionHostProcess.js:501:4260)
	at tHe.logIt (github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:2774:2124)
	at /github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:1119:2241
	at Array.forEach (<anonymous>)
	at Wmt._logIt (github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:1119:2228)
	at Wmt.debug (github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:1119:2293)
	at n.debug (github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:1119:2786)
	at m4t.remove (github.copilot-chat-0.40.1/dist/extension.js:2212:44391)
```

### Root Cause

The `m4t.remove` handler's logging pipeline does not guard against the debug channel being closed. During extension host shutdown, VS Code closes the RPC debug channel before disposing extension subscriptions (filed as microsoft/vscode#303916). When tool disposables fire, `m4t.remove` calls `debug()` which throws.

### Proposed Fix

Add a try-catch in the logging pipeline used by `m4t.remove` (and other shutdown-time code paths) to gracefully handle closed channels:

```typescript
// In tHe.logIt or Wmt._logIt:
try {
    // existing debug logging
} catch (err) {
    // Silently ignore during shutdown — channel already closed
}
```

### Environment

- Copilot Chat: 0.40.1
- VS Code: 1.99.x (Remote SSH)
- OS: Linux (RHEL)

### Related

- microsoft/vscode#303916 — VS Code core shutdown ordering issue (root cause on VS Code side)

author: Chudesnov
text:
github.copilot-chat missing linux-arm64 pty.node prebuild — breaks Copilot CLI integration in linux/arm64 devcontainers

## Summary

The `@github/copilot/sdk` package bundled in `github.copilot-chat` only ships a `darwin-arm64` prebuild for `pty.node` (from `node-pty`). The `linux-arm64` prebuild is absent, causing `CopilotCLISession` to fail entirely on linux/arm64 containers:

```
[CopilotCLISession] Failed to load @github/copilot/sdk: Error: Failed to load native module: pty.node,
checked: build/Release, build/Debug, prebuilds/linux-arm64:
Error: Cannot find module './prebuilds/linux-arm64/pty.node'
```

## Affected environment

- **Extension**: `github.copilot-chat` v0.39.2 (latest as of 2026-03-23)
- **Platform**: linux/arm64 (e.g. VSCode devcontainer on Apple Silicon via Colima/Docker)
- **Impact**: `CopilotCLISession`, `CopilotCLIAgents`, and `CopilotCLIModels` all fail to initialize. Copilot chat completions still work, but the Copilot CLI agent integration is completely broken.

## Root cause

The `node-pty` upstream fix for linux-arm64 cross-compilation was merged in [microsoft/node-pty#857](https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty/pull/857) (January 2026), resolving [microsoft/node-pty#860](https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty/issues/860) where the linux-arm64 prebuild was either missing or compiled as x86-64. That fix is in the `1.2.0` milestone.

`@github/copilot/sdk` appears to still be pinned to a version of `node-pty` that does not include a correct `linux-arm64` prebuild.

## Expected behavior

`prebuilds/linux-arm64/pty.node` should be present in `@github/copilot/sdk` so the extension loads correctly in linux/arm64 devcontainers.

## Workaround

We are currently working around this in our devcontainer by using a `NODE_OPTIONS=--require` preload that intercepts `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for `pty.node` requests from vscode-server extensions and copies a locally-compiled binary to the expected path. This is fragile and should not be necessary once upstream ships the correct prebuild.

## Request

Please update `@github/copilot/sdk` to a version of `node-pty` that includes the linux-arm64 prebuild (node-pty ≥ 1.2.0 once stable, or vendor the binary directly). This would unblock VS Code devcontainer users on Apple Silicon (and any linux/arm64 CI environments).

text:
I've been using the alpha for the past 2 weeks, and I'm blown away. Copilot guesses the exact code I want to write about one in ten times, and the rest of the time it suggests something rather good, or completely off. But when it guesses right, it feels like it's reading my mind.

It's really like pair programming, even though I'm coding alone. I have a better understanding of my own code, and I tend to give better names and descriptions to my methods. I write better code, documentation, and tests.

Copilot has made me a better programmer. No kidding. This is a huge achievement. Kudos to the GitHub Copilot team!

author: cbsks
text:
I don't think we need to start looking for new career paths yet. This example has a few bugs and it took me longer to track them down than it would have to write it myself:

  #!/bin/bash
  # List all python source files which are more than 1KB and contain the word "copilot".
  find . \
    -name "*.py" \
    -size +1000 \
    -exec grep -n copilot {}\;
"-exec grep -n copilot {}\;" needs to have a space before the semicolon otherwise find fails with "find: missing argument to '-exec'".

The "1000" in "-size +1000" has a unit of 512 byte blocks so it is looking for files that are greater than 512000 bytes, not 1KB. This would be very easy to miss in a code review and is one of those terrible bugs that causes the code to mostly work, but not quite.

https://linux.die.net/man/1/find

author: inimino
text:
I'm amazed to see how positive the overall response is to this idea. Almost as if programmers think that writing programs is the worst part of the job and ready to be automated away.

As someone more aligned with the Dijkstra perspective, this seems to me like one of the single worst ideas I've ever seen in this domain.

We already have IDEs and other tools leading to an increase in boilerplate and the acceptance of it because they make it easier to manage. I can only imagine what kinds of codebases a product like this could lead to. Someone will produce 5000 lines of code in a day for a new feature, but only read 2000 of those lines. Folks that still expect you to only check in code you understand and can explain will become a minority.

I wonder how long it will be until someone sets up the rest of the feedback loop and starts putting up github projects made of nothing but code from this tool, and it can start to feed on itself.

Cargo-cult programming has always been a problem, but now we're explicitly building tools for it.

author: azinman2
text:
I worry about auto-complete on a more philosophical level. I’ve noticed with gmail that it’ll often suggest it’s way of either replying to an email or completing a sentence even though I’d never actually use those words in that situation, simply because it’s easier.

It’s a pretty bad feedback loop that robs us of our independent thought by way of falling victim to laziness, a fundamental human weakness. You can imagine something where in this case the code autocomplete is so large that you really want to make that autocompletion work, even if you know it’s not elegant or possibly even correct code… or maybe it’s just repetitive and not abstracted well, but here it is autocompleted and done so why would you fight that?

If we continue abstracting more and more of this way, based upon datasets that are averaged across everyone, we lose the individual in favor of the masses, bringing us all down to a common denominator.

If we must lose our humanity to the machine, I’d at least like to see an autocomplete from Peter Norvig’s code, or writing from particularly effective communicators or famous authors.

author: CityOfThrowaway
text:
This is very impressive!

OpenAI’s tech opens an ethical Pandora’s box:

1. It’s clear that the raw inputs to all of OpenAI’s outputs originated with real, human creativity.

2. So, in a sense, OpenAI is laundering creativity. It reads in creative works, does complicated (and, yes, groundbreaking) transformations, and produces an output that is hard to trace to any particular source.

3. Yet, isn’t that effectively what human brains do too? Perhaps OpenAI lacks the capacity for true invention, but I’d argue that most people live their whole lives without a meaningful creative contribution as well.

All told, I don’t have a good framework for thinking about the ethics here. So instead, I’ll simply say:

Wow.
